chapters.file: ch16 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
chapters.relation: Richard Greene analyzes The King of Comedy's Rupert Pupkin, who kidnaps talk-show host Jerry Landers to force his way onto TV and emerges a celebrity, calling this the 'Pupkin gambit' (harming others and oneself to secure an overwhelming personal payoff). Distinguishing internalist accounts of rationality (Plato's well-ordered soul, Kant's universalizable maxims) from an externalist one, Greene argues the gambit is irrational for a sane agent like the financier Michael Milken but rational for Pupkin via a Pascal's-wager structure: because Pupkin is delusional, even imagined success satisfies his desire, so the wager has huge upside and no real downside for him. He also invokes ethical egoism to show unethical acts can still be assessed for self-interested rationality.

chapters.file: ch17 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
ch18 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
chapters.relation: Karen D. Hoffman reads The Last Temptation of Christ and Bringing Out the Dead through Sartre's distinction between the for-itself (transcendence) and the in-itself (immanence), arguing both reluctant saviors are tempted into bad faith. Scorsese's Jesus, tempted on the cross to abandon his mission and live as an ordinary husband and father, passively drifts toward a life of pure immanence that denies his human transcendence, until (following Kazantzakis's 'sprouting of wings' image via Judas) he reclaims his choice to be crucified. Frank Pierce inversely faces a false transcendence—the temptation to think of himself as God, or to escape via drugs, violence, or suicide—and resists it, allowing the vegetative Mr. Burke to die. Hoffman frames avoiding either exaggeration as the path to authentic Sartrean humanity and grace.

chapters.file: ch19 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
chapters.relation: Paul A. Cantor argues that The Aviator, unusually for Hollywood, is a libertarian celebration of the entrepreneur, turning billionaire Howard Hughes into a Scorsese underdog battling the establishment. Drawing on Adam Smith and the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises, Cantor reads Hughes's willingness to risk his own money on Hell's Angels and TWA, his visionary anticipation of talkies and jets, and his Senate-hearing fight against the Pan Am/Senator Brewster monopoly as a dramatization of the true risk-taking entrepreneur versus the mere manager. The 'socialist dinner party' with the aristocratic Hepburns and Hughes's defeat of government-backed monopoly illustrate Smith's suspicion of merchants seeking privilege and his invisible-hand claim that self-interested competition, not those who 'trade for the publick good,' best serves the public.

chapters.file: ch20 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
chapters.relation: Richard Gilmore reads After Hours as a nocturnal katabasis in which office worker Paul Hackett is repeatedly offered, and repeatedly fails at, authentic encounter with the SoHo women and their artworks (Kiki's papier-mache man, the plaster-of-paris bagel). Using Levinas's totality-versus-infinity and the ethics of conversation, Kant's two worlds of interest and disinterested aesthetic judgment, and Dewey's Art as Experience, Gilmore argues that art and sex alike (per Picasso and Nagel's 'double reciprocal incarnation') demand abandoning one's 'logic of the same' to perceive the other. Foucault's disciplinary kronos-time versus kairos, and Zizek's anamorphic spot, frame Paul's entrapment in solipsism until, encased as a literal artwork and reborn at the office gates, he finally offers himself to June.

chapters.file: ch21 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
chapters.relation: Judith Barad explains the puzzling elements of Kundun—the compassion for enemies, the child taken from his parents, the swept-away sand mandala, the sky burial—through Tibetan Buddhist ethics, arguing it closely parallels Greek and Roman Stoicism. She reads the young Dalai Lama's growth into compassion and nonviolence toward Mao and the Chinese alongside Epictetus's teaching that only our own judgments, not others' acts, can harm us, and that we must restrain desire and attachment. The Four Noble Truths reframe the film: because all things (including the self) are impermanent and interconnected, the destruction of the mandala and the feeding of the father's corpse to vultures enact detachment, and true liberation via the Eightfold Path is self-won inner peace that China cannot seize.

chapters.file: ch22 - The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese.md
chapters.relation: R. Barton Palmer situates Scorsese as a 'saint of cinema' whose Emersonian transcendentalism—the 'influx of light and power' breaking through the material everyday—pervades even his commercial films, focusing on Bringing Out the Dead against Casino and Taxi Driver. He traces the Bressonian 'decisive moment' and Schrader's Calvinist-Jansenist reading of predestination and grace (Ace Rothstein's inexplicable survival in Casino, the elect/damned divide of Taxi Driver and Hardcore), where Travis Bickle remains 'God's lonely man' beyond redemption. Palmer argues Scorsese departs from Schrader's bleak limited atonement: Frank Pierce earns communal grace through willed effort, releasing Mary's father, asking forgiveness, and ending in a Pieta embrace that affirms redemption is attainable within the material world.

holes.name: Ludwig von Mises
holes.what: Austrian-school economist and libertarian social philosopher who theorized the entrepreneur as risk-bearing speculator and defended free markets against socialism.
holes.why: Chapter 19 builds its whole libertarian reading of The Aviator on Mises's Human Action account of the entrepreneur versus the manager, which no taxonomy philosopher covers (Adam Smith is used only for the invisible hand).

holes.name: The Entrepreneur (risk-bearing and market discovery)
holes.what: The libertarian/Austrian idea that the true entrepreneur profits by risking his own capital on an anticipation of future demand, a function distinct from mere management.
holes.why: The chapter's central applied concept—Hughes as visionary entrepreneur risking 'his own money'—has no taxonomy concept; invisible-hand captures only part of the argument.
